extracted.intended_audience: readers of moral aphorisms, students/scholars of La Rochefoucauld and 17th-century maxims
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and present the moral maxims and reflective rules appearing in La Rochefoucauld's Maxims (first/second/third supplements) and the accompanying reflections on confidence and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward death
rubrics_metrics.description: The wisest and bravest are those who take the best means to avoid reflecting on it; the necessity of dying created all the constancy of philosophers; the glory of dying with courage, the hope of being regretted, the desire to leave behind us a good reputation... are resources which should not be passed over, but they should affect us in the same proportion as a single shelter affects those who in war storm a fortress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual commentary: do not mistake distant theorizing about death for true courage when it is imminent; self-deception is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: I. Self-love definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-love is the love of self, and of all things for self. It makes men self-worshippers, and if fortune permits them, causes them to tyrannize over others; ... It is made up of contraries. It is imperious and obedient, sincere and false, piteous and cruel, timid and bold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edition of 1665, No. 1. Long explanatory passage describing mechanisms and perversities of self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: II. Passions as blood temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are only the different degrees of the heat or coldness of the blood.

rubrics_metrics.name: III. Moderation in good fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation in good fortune is but apprehension of the shame which follows upon haughtiness, or a fear of losing what we have.

rubrics_metrics.name: IV. Moderation analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation is like temperance in eating; we could eat more but we fear to make ourselves ill.

rubrics_metrics.name: V. Projection of faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Everybody finds that to abuse in another which he finds worthy of abuse in himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: VI. Pride and haughtiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride, as if tired of its artifices and its different metamorphoses, after having solely filled the divers parts of the comedy of life, exhibits itself with its natural face, and is discovered by haughtiness; so much so that we may truly say that haughtiness is but the flash and open declaration of pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: VII. Knowing point of misery
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind of happiness is to know exactly at what point to be miserable.

rubrics_metrics.name: VIII. Peace of mind comes from within
rubrics_metrics.description: When we do not find peace of mind (REPOS) in ourselves it is useless to seek it elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: IX. Answer for one's fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be able to answer for one's fortune, so as to be able to answer for what we shall do.

rubrics_metrics.name: X. Love animates the lover
rubrics_metrics.description: Love is to the soul of him who loves, what the soul is to the body which it animates.

rubrics_metrics.name: XI. On justice of complaints about inconstancy
rubrics_metrics.description: As one is never at liberty to love or to cease from loving, the lover cannot with justice complain of the inconstancy of his mistress, nor she of the fickleness of her lover.

rubrics_metrics.name: XII. Judges' moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice in those judges who are moderate is but a love of their place.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIII. Tired of loving
rubrics_metrics.description: When we are tired of loving we are quite content if our mistress should become faithless, to loose us from our fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV. Joy at friends' happiness arises from self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: The first impulse of joy which we feel at the happiness of our friends arises neither from our natural goodness nor from friendship; it is the result of self-love, which flatters us with being lucky in our own turn, or in reaping something from the good fortune of our friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV. Mixed feelings at friends' adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the adversity of our best friends we always find something which is not wholly displeasing to us.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI. Keep other people's secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: How shall we hope that another person will keep our secret if we do not keep it ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVII. Self-love changes perception of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-love... changes other objects... when a female is adverse to us... self-love pronounces on her actions with all the severity of justice; ... If however the same female becomes favourable to us... our sole self interest gives her back the lustre which our hatred deprived her of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No date or number given for this maxim (provided in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: XVIII. Idle persons press heavily on others
rubrics_metrics.description: There are none who press so heavily on others as the lazy ones, when they have satisfied their idleness, and wish to appear industrious.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIX. Blindness from pride
rubrics_metrics.description: The blindness of men is the most dangerous effect of their pride; it seems to nourish and augment it, it deprives us of knowledge of remedies which can solace our miseries and can cure our faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX. Least reason when despairing of others
rubrics_metrics.description: One has never less reason than when one despairs of finding it in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXI. Philosophers and pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers, and Seneca above all, have not diminished crimes by their precepts; they have only used them in the building up of pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXII. Little friendship to miss cooling
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a proof of little friendship not to perceive the growing coolness of that of our friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXIII. Wisdom limited to ordinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The most wise may be so in indifferent and ordinary matters, but they are seldom so in their most serious affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXIV. Subtle folly from subtle wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The most subtle folly grows out of the most subtle wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXV. Sobriety defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Sobriety is the love of health, or an incapacity to eat much.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXVI. Forgetting things when tired of talking
rubrics_metrics.description: We never forget things so well as when we are tired of talking of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXVII. Praise roots practice of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The praise bestowed upon us is at least useful in rooting us in the practice of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXVIII. Self-love shields the flatterer
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-love takes care to prevent him whom we flatter from being him who most flatters us.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXIX. Praise and blame from interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Men only blame vice and praise virtue from interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXX. Kinds of anger
rubrics_metrics.description: We make no difference in the kinds of anger, although there is that which is light and almost innocent, which arises from warmth of complexion, temperament, and another very criminal, which is, to speak properly, the fury of pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXI. Great souls defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Great souls are not those who have fewer passions and more virtues than the common, but those only who have greater designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXII. Kings and value of men
rubrics_metrics.description: Kings do with men as with pieces of money; they make them bear what value they will, and one is forced to receive them according to their currency value, and not at their true worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXIII. Self-love makes more cruel
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural ferocity makes fewer people cruel than self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXIV. Virtues as art of appearing
rubrics_metrics.description: One may say of all our virtues as an Italian poet says of the propriety of women, that it is often merely the art of appearing chaste.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXV. Crimes excused by brilliancy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are crimes which become innocent and even glorious by their brilliancy, their number, or their excess; thus it happens that public robbery is called financial skill, and the unjust capture of provinces is called a conquest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1665, No. 192. (Satirical note: some biblical/historical exceptions are glossed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXVI. No excess of good or evil in man
rubrics_metrics.description: One never finds in man good or evil in excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXVII. Incapable of great crimes distrustful
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are incapable of committing great crimes do not easily suspect others.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXVIII. Funerals' pomp for living vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The pomp of funerals concerns rather the vanity of the living, than the honour of the dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXIX. Providence and ordered course
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever variety and change appears in the world, we may remark a secret chain, and a regulated order of all time by Providence, which makes everything follow in due rank and fall into its destined course.

rubrics_metrics.name: XL. Intrepidity in conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrepidity should sustain the heart in conspiracies in place of valour which alone furnishes all the firmness which is necessary for the perils of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLI. Origin of victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who wish to define victory by her birth will be tempted to imitate the poets, and to call her the Daughter of Heaven... Truly she is produced from an infinity of actions, which... produce a good so great and general.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLII. Courage tested by danger
rubrics_metrics.description: That man who has never been in danger cannot answer for his courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLIII. Bounds on gratitude vs desires
rubrics_metrics.description: We more often place bounds on our gratitude than on our desires and our hopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLIV. Imitation unhappy
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is always unhappy, for all which is counterfeit displeases by the very things which charm us when they are original (Naturelles).

rubrics_metrics.name: XLV. Regret friends by our needs
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not regret the loss of our friends according to their merits, but according to OUR wants, and the opinion with which we believed we had impressed them of our worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVI. Commonness of cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very hard to separate the general goodness spread all over the world from great cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVII. Being always good requires deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: For us to be always good, others should believe that they cannot behave wickedly to us with impunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII. Confidence to please can displease
rubrics_metrics.description: A confidence in being able to please is often an infallible means of being displeasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLIX. Self-confidence arises from confidence in others
rubrics_metrics.description: The confidence we have in ourselves arises in a great measure from that that we have in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: L. General revolution of tastes and fortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a general revolution which changes the tastes of the mind as well as the fortunes of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: LI. Truth as foundation of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is foundation and the reason of the perfection of beauty, for of whatever stature a thing may be, it cannot be beautiful and perfect unless it be truly that she should be, and possess truly all that she should have.

rubrics_metrics.name: LII. Brilliance of the unfinished
rubrics_metrics.description: There are fine things which are more brilliant when unfinished than when finished too much.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIII. Magnanimity as proud mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnanimity is a noble effort of pride which makes a man master of himself, to make him master of all things.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV. Luxury presages fall
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury and too refined a policy in states are a sure presage of their fall, because all parties looking after their own interest turn away from the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: LV. Idleness as hidden danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all passions that which is least known to us is idleness; she is the most ardent and evil of all, although her violence may be insensible, and the evils she causes concealed; ... idleness, like a beatitude of the soul, consoles us for all losses and fills the vacancy of all our wants.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVI. Fondness for reading others' characters
rubrics_metrics.description: We are very fond of reading others' characters, but we do not like to be read ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVII. Burdensome regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: What a tiresome malady is that which forces one to preserve your health by a severe regimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVIII. Love easier to take than to leave
rubrics_metrics.description: It is much easier to take love when one is free, than to get rid of it after having taken it.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX. Women surrender more from weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Women for the most part surrender themselves more from weakness than from passion. Whence it is that bold and pushing men succeed better than others, although they are not so loveable.

rubrics_metrics.name: LX. Not to love is a means of being beloved
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to love is in love, an infallible means of being beloved.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXI. Sincerity requested by lovers
rubrics_metrics.description: The sincerity which lovers and mistresses ask that both should know when they cease to love each other, arises much less from a wish to be warned of the cessation of love, than from a desire to be assured that they are beloved although no one denies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXII. Love compared to fever
rubrics_metrics.description: The most just comparison of love is that of a fever, and we have no power over either, as to its violence or its duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXIII. Skill of the least skilful
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest skill of the least skilful is to know how to submit to the direction of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXIV. Fear to see loved ones after flirting
rubrics_metrics.description: We always fear to see those whom we love when we have been flirting with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXV. Consolation for faults
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to console ourselves for our faults when we have strength enough to own them.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXVI. Interest as soul of self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest is the soul of self-love, in as much as when the body deprived of its soul is without sight, feeling or knowledge, ... so self-love, riven so to speak from its interest, neither sees, nor hears, nor smells, nor moves; ... a man becomes dull or bright just as his own interest is near to him or distant from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter To Madame De Sable, Ms., Fol. 211.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXVII. Fear of maxims that bare the heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Why we cry out so much against maxims which lay bare the heart of man, is because we fear that our own heart shall be laid bare.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXVIII. Hope and fear inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Hope and fear are inseparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To Madame De Sable, Ms., Fol. 222, MAX. 168.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXIX. Hazard life to escape dishonour
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a common thing to hazard life to escape dishonour; but, when this is done, the actor takes very little pain to make the enterprise succeed ... those who hazard their lives to take a city or to conquer a province are better officers... than they who merely expose themselves to vindicate their honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter To M. Esprit, Ms., Fol. 173, MAX. 219.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXX. Taste changes, will the same
rubrics_metrics.description: The taste changes, but the will remains the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To Madame De Sable, Fol. 223, Max. 252.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXI. Power of women beloved over men
rubrics_metrics.description: The power which women whom we love have over us is greater than that which we have over ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To The Same, Ms., Fol. 211, Max. 259.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXII. We believe what we wish
rubrics_metrics.description: That which makes us believe so easily that others have defects is that we all so easily believe what we wish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To The Same, Ms., Fol. 223, Max. 397.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXIII. Few know how to be old
rubrics_metrics.description: I am perfectly aware that good sense and fine wit are tedious to every age, but tastes are not always the same, and what is good at one time will not seem so at another. This makes me think that few persons know how to be old.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXIV. God permitted self-love as punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: God has permitted, to punish man for his original sin, that he should be so fond of his self-love, that he should be tormented by it in all the actions of his life.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXV. Limited gaiety of a lacquey
rubrics_metrics.description: And so far it seems to me the philosophy of a lacquey can go; I believe that all gaity in that state of life is very doubtful indeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To Madame De Sable, Fol. 161, Max. 504. (Comments on footman's merriment before execution.)

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXVI. Wish to be devout vs humble
rubrics_metrics.description: Many persons wish to be devout; but no one wishes to be humble.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXVII. Labour eases mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The labour of the body frees us from the pains of the mind, and thus makes the poor happy.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXVIII. True penitential sorrows unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: True penitential sorrows (mortifications) are those which are not known, vanity renders the others easy enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXIX. Humility as altar
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility is the altar upon which God wishes that we should offer him his sacrifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXX. Few things for wise man's happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Few things are needed to make a wise man happy; nothing can make a fool content; that is why most men are miserable.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXI. Appear happy vs be happy
rubrics_metrics.description: We trouble ourselves less to become happy, than to make others believe we are so.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXII. Extinguishing first desire
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more easy to extinguish the first desire than to satisfy those which follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXIII. Wisdom to soul as health to body
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom is to the soul what health is to the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXIV. Great ones cannot command health
rubrics_metrics.description: The great ones of the earth can neither command health of body nor repose of mind, and they buy always at too dear a price the good they can acquire.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXV. Examine happiness of possessors
rubrics_metrics.description: Before strongly desiring anything we should examine what happiness he has who possesses it.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXVI. True friend is greatest good
rubrics_metrics.description: A true friend is the greatest of all goods, and that of which we think least of acquiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXVII. Lovers blind to faults until enchantment ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Lovers do not wish to see the faults of their mistresses until their enchantment is at an end.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXVIII. Prudence and love incompatible
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence and love are not made for each other; in the ratio that love increases, prudence diminishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: LXXXIX. Pleasing to have jealous wife
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes pleasing to a husband to have a jealous wife; he hears her always speaking of the beloved object.

rubrics_metrics.name: XC. Woman with virtue and love pitied
rubrics_metrics.description: How much is a woman to be pitied who is at the same time possessed of virtue and love!

rubrics_metrics.name: XCI. Better not to enter than to conquer
rubrics_metrics.description: The wise man finds it better not to enter the encounter than to conquer.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCII. Study men more than books
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more necessary to study men than books.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCIII. Good and evil come to extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Good and evil ordinarily come to those who have most of one or the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCIV. Native country accent dwells in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The accent and character of one's native country dwells in the mind and heart as on the tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCV. Qualities discovered by chance
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of men have qualities which, like those of plants, are discovered by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCVI. Good woman hidden treasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A good woman is a hidden treasure; he who discovers her will do well not to boast about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCVII. Women weep to show they were loved
rubrics_metrics.description: Most women do not weep for the loss of a lover to show that they have been loved so much as to show that they are worth being loved.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCVIII. Virtuous women weary of part
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many virtuous women who are weary of the part they have played.

rubrics_metrics.name: XCIX. Mistaken love-for-love belief
rubrics_metrics.description: If we think we love for love's sake we are much mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: C. Constraint for constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The restraint we lay upon ourselves to be constant, is not much better than an inconstancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: CI. Avoided are those we should fear
rubrics_metrics.description: There are those who avoid our jealousy, of whom we ought to be jealous.

rubrics_metrics.name: CII. Jealousy born with love
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is always born with love, but does not always die with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: CIII. Hard to know when loved ceases if we love too much
rubrics_metrics.description: When we love too much it is difficult to discover when we have ceased to be beloved.

rubrics_metrics.name: CIV. Speak of wives but not of self
rubrics_metrics.description: We know very well that we should not talk about our wives, but we do not remember that it is not so well to speak of ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV. Chance reveals us
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance makes us known to others and to ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: CVI. Few people of good sense except our own opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: We find very few people of good sense, except those who are of our own opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: CVII. Praise good hearts of those who admire us
rubrics_metrics.description: We commonly praise the good hearts of those who admire us.

rubrics_metrics.name: CVIII. Blame self to be praised
rubrics_metrics.description: Man only blames himself in order that he may be praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: CIX. Little minds wounded by small things
rubrics_metrics.description: Little minds are wounded by the smallest things.

rubrics_metrics.name: CX. Faults in good light please
rubrics_metrics.description: There are certain faults which placed in a good light please more than perfection itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXI. Bitterness at being outwitted
rubrics_metrics.description: That which makes us so bitter against those who do us a shrewd turn, is because they think themselves more clever than we are.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXII. Bored by those we bored
rubrics_metrics.description: We are always bored by those whom we bore.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXIII. Harm from others less than from ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The harm that others do us is often less than that we do ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXIV. Difficult to speak well when ashamed of silence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is never more difficult to speak well than when we are ashamed of being silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXV. Faults pardonable if avowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Those faults are always pardonable that we have the courage to avow.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXVI. Penetration fault
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest fault of penetration is not that it goes to the bottom of a matter--but beyond it.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXVII. Advice vs wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: We give advice, but we cannot give the wisdom to profit by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXVIII. Merit and taste decline together
rubrics_metrics.description: When our merit declines, our taste declines also.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXIX. Fortune discovers vices and virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune discovers our vices and our virtues, as the light makes objects plain to the sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXX. Actions like rhymed verse-ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Our actions are like rhymed verse-ends (Bouts-Rimes) which everyone turns as he pleases.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXXI. Deceptive belief of being beloved
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing more natural, nor more deceptive, than to believe that we are beloved.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXXII. Prefer those we benefited
rubrics_metrics.description: We would rather see those to whom we have done a benefit, than those who have done us one.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXXIII. Harder to hide opinions than feign others
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more difficult to hide the opinions we have than to feign those which we have not.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXXIV. Renewed friendships need more care
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewed friendships require more care than those that have never been broken.

rubrics_metrics.name: CXXV. One who pleases nobody vs pleases all
rubrics_metrics.description: A man to whom no one is pleasing is much more unhappy than one who pleases nobody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on Confidence (I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is an openness of heart... Confidence leaves us less liberty, its rules are stricter, it requires more prudence and reticence... Confidence always pleases those who receive it. It is a tribute we pay to their merit, a deposit we commit to their trust, a pledge which gives them a claim upon us...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'REFLECTIONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS, BY THE DUKE DE LA ROCHEFOUCAULD' — 'I. On Confidence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on Confidence (II) - confidants selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Most frequently we make confidants from vanity, a love of talking, a wish to win the confidence of others, and make an exchange of secrets. Some may have a motive for confiding in us... Others whose fidelity we know trust nothing to us, but we confide in them by choice and inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: do not give half confidences; be discreet; keep secrets intact; prefer silence to partial revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on Confidence (III) - keeping secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: We should make it a rule never to have half confidences. They always embarrass those who give them, and dissatisfy those who receive them. It is far safer and more honest to tell nothing than to be silent when we have begun to tell. Everyone agrees that a secret should be kept intact, but everyone does not agree as to the nature and importance of secresy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for conduct: when a friend entrusts you, preserve it completely; avoid half-revelations that invite curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on Confidence (IV) - test of fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: With those friends whose truth we know we have the closest intimacy. ... They may have elsewhere learnt what we have promised not to tell. It is not in our power to tell them what has been entrusted to us, though it might tend to their interest to know it. ... His first duty is to rigidly keep his trust in its entirety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forced between preserving a friend's trust and other pressures, sacrifice the relationship rather than the secret if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Difference of Character (I) - genius qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Although all the qualities of mind may be united in a great genius, yet there are some which are special and peculiar to him; his views are unlimited; he always acts uniformly and with the same activity; he sees distant objects as if present; ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive distinctions between types of minds; guidance for appraisal of mental qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Difference of Character (II) - kinds of wit and mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A lofty mind always thinks nobly... A clever, pliant, winning mind knows how to avoid and overcome difficulties... There is a difference between an ardent and a brilliant mind, a fiery spirit travels further and faster, while a brilliant mind is sparkling, attractive, accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions to evaluate temperament and appropriateness for different social roles; satire and raillery have risks and uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Difference of Character (III) - satire and raillery
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is at once the most agreeable and most dangerous of mental qualities. It always pleases when it is refined, but we always fear those who use it too much, yet satire should be allowed when unmixed with spite, and when the person satirised can join in the satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: use satire sparingly, without malice, and where the target can tolerate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Difference of Character (IV) - cunning vs acute mind
rubrics_metrics.description: An acute mind and a cunning mind are very dissimilar. The first always pleases; it is unfettered, it perceives the most delicate and sees the most imperceptible matters. A cunning spirit never goes straight, it endeavours to secure its object by byeways and short cuts. This conduct is soon found out, it always gives rise to distrust and never reaches greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value straightforward acuity over furtive cunning when judging character or leadership potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Difference of Character (V) - 'Bel Esprit' misapplied
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'Bel Esprit' is much perverted, for all that one can say of the different kinds of mind meet together in the 'Bel Esprit.' Yet as the epithet is bestowed on an infinite number of bad poets and tedious authors, it is more often used to ridicule than to praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: labels of praise can be diluted; evaluate substance not epithet.
